One of them, A B C, is drawn in the accent color; B C D ties it, and no four nodes are all linked. The card gives the clique number 3." width="100%"} The clique number `ω(G)` is the size of the largest clique in the graph, where a clique is a set of nodes that are all directly connected to one another. This is a fundamental graph invariant used in graph theory and combinatorial optimization. It is a compact summary of how tightly knit the densest part of a network is. Typical uses: - comparing the "core tightness" of several networks with a single number - giving a lower bound on the chromatic number (any coloring needs at least `ω(G)` colors), which matters for scheduling and register-allocation style problems - quickly checking whether a graph contains a triangle (`ω(G) >= 3`) or a larger complete subgraph The value equals `len(graph.maximum_clique())`; use `maximum_clique()` if you also need to know which nodes form the clique. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of the maximum clique. Returns `0` for empty graphs and `1` for graphs that have nodes but no edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The clique number $\omega(G)$ is one of the fundamental graph invariants and is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard to compute in general. Extremes are easy to reason about, though: for the complete graph $\omega(K_n) = n$; for any bipartite graph $\omega(G) \le 2$, because a third vertex would need to be adjacent to two already-adjacent vertices, contradicting bipartiteness; and for any triangle-free graph the same $\omega(G) \le 2$ bound holds. The implementation shares the Bron-Kerbosch enumeration behind `find_cliques()` and inherits its $O(3^{n/3})$ worst-case bound. Undirected graphs only. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle is itself a clique of three nodes, so its clique number is `3`: ::: {#3c3ee025 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.clique_number() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A path's largest clique is just a single edge, since no three nodes form a triangle: ::: {#0d0032ab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.clique_number() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: An empty graph has clique number `0`: ::: {#d89ab36a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph(directed=False).clique_number() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph `K_n` always has clique number `n`: ::: {#198a03b3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=7) graph.clique_number() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 7 ``` ::: ::: Bipartite graphs can never contain a triangle, so their clique number never exceeds `2`: ::: {#77dc460c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D")]) ) graph.clique_number() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 2 ``` ::: :::
